title: Spherical Law of Cosines
description: The spherical analogue of the planar law of cosines: cos(c) = cos(a)cos(b) + sin(a)sin(b)cos(C), for a spherical triangle on the unit sphere S² with arc-length sides a, b, c and dihedral angle C opposite side c. Proved using inner product decomposition of unit vectors in ℝ³.

overview.historicalContext:
The spherical law of cosines is one of the fundamental results of spherical trigonometry, with origins in Islamic mathematics. Al-Battani (~900 CE) gave early forms, and the result was systematically developed by Regiomontanus (1464), Euler (1781), and formalized in Todhunter's comprehensive treatise (1886).

For a spherical triangle on the unit sphere S² with arc-length sides a, b, c (measuring the central angle subtended) and dihedral angle C opposite side c:

  cos(c) = cos(a)·cos(b) + sin(a)·sin(b)·cos(C)

This is the curved-space analogue of the planar law of cosines c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cos(C). In the small-angle limit (a, b, c → 0), the spherical formula reduces to the planar formula via Taylor expansion: cos(x) ≈ 1 - x²/2 and sin(x) ≈ x.

Spherical trigonometry was essential for celestial navigation, astronomy, and cartography — the core computational tool of the Age of Exploration. Today it remains fundamental in geodesy, satellite navigation (GPS), crystallography, and computer graphics.
overview.problemStatement:
**The Spherical Law of Cosines**: For a spherical triangle on S² with arc-length sides a, b, c and dihedral angle C at vertex C:

$$\cos c = \cos a \cdot \cos b + \sin a \cdot \sin b \cdot \cos C$$

Equivalently, for unit vectors A, B, C ∈ S² ⊂ ℝ³:
$$\langle A, B \rangle = \langle A, C \rangle \langle B, C \rangle + \langle \text{proj}^\perp_C A,\, \text{proj}^\perp_C B \rangle$$

where proj⊥_C denotes orthogonal projection onto the plane perpendicular to C.
overview.text: A Lean 4 formalization of the spherical law of cosines using inner products in ℝ³. The proof represents points on the unit sphere S² as unit vectors in EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3), defines arc length as arccos(⟨u,v⟩), and derives the spherical law of cosines from a fundamental inner product decomposition lemma. The formalization covers 24 theorems across 341 lines with 0 sorries and 0 axioms.
overview.proofStrategy:
The proof proceeds through an elegant inner product decomposition:

**1. Setup**: Unit vectors A, B, C ∈ ℝ³ represent vertices on S². Arc lengths are defined as arcLength(u,v) = arccos(⟨u,v⟩).

**2. Orthogonal Projection**: For unit n, define proj⊥(v, n) = v - ⟨v,n⟩·n, the component of v perpendicular to n.

**3. Key Identity**: inner_decomposition proves:
  ⟨u, v⟩ = ⟨u, n⟩·⟨v, n⟩ + ⟨proj⊥(u,n), proj⊥(v,n)⟩

This follows from bilinearity: expand ⟨u - ⟨u,n⟩n, v - ⟨v,n⟩n⟩ and use ⟨n,n⟩ = 1.

**4. Trigonometric Translation**: ⟨u,n⟩ = cos(arcLength) by construction, and ‖proj⊥(u,n)‖ = sin(arcLength) via Pythagorean identity. The inner product of projections becomes sin(b)·sin(a)·cos(C).

**5. Result**: cos(c) = cos(b)·cos(a) + sin(b)·sin(a)·cos(C).
keyInsights: The inner product decomposition ⟨u,v⟩ = ⟨u,n⟩⟨v,n⟩ + ⟨u⊥,v⊥⟩ is the algebraic heart of spherical trigonometry — it decomposes the dot product into 'along n' and 'perpendicular to n' components, mirroring how the spherical law of cosines separates the geodesic distance into contributions from the two adjacent sides and the included angle

The perpendicular projection proj⊥(v,n) = v - ⟨v,n⟩n geometrically gives the component of v in the tangent plane to S² at n. Its norm equals sin(arc length) because ‖v‖² = ⟨v,n⟩² + ‖v⊥‖² gives 1 = cos²θ + ‖v⊥‖², so ‖v⊥‖ = sin θ

The proof avoids coordinates entirely — it works in abstract inner product space ℝ³, using only bilinearity, symmetry, and ⟨n,n⟩ = 1. This makes it dimension-independent: the same decomposition works on S^n for any n
The small-angle limit cos(c) ≈ 1-c²/2 shows how the spherical formula reduces to c² ≈ a²+b²-2ab·cos(C), connecting spherical and Euclidean geometry via curvature → 0
Degenerate cases (when a vertex coincides with another) are handled: proj⊥(n,n) = 0, so the cross term vanishes, giving cos(0) = cos(b)·cos(a) as expected
prerequisites: Trigonometric functions (arccos, sin, cos) and Pythagorean identity
Unit vectors and the unit sphere S² ⊂ ℝ³

sections.title: Part I: Unit Vectors in ℝ³
sections.summary: Defines Vec3 = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3) and IsUnitVec. Proves inner product bounds for unit vectors: |⟨u,v⟩| ≤ 1, ⟨u,v⟩ ≤ 1, ⟨u,v⟩ ≥ -1.

sections.title: Part II: Arc Length on the Sphere
sections.summary: Defines arcLength(u,v) = arccos(⟨u,v⟩). Proves non-negativity, bound ≤ π, cos(arcLength) = ⟨u,v⟩, self-distance = 0, and symmetry.

sections.title: Part III: Spherical Triangle
sections.summary: Defines SphericalTriangle structure with three unit vector vertices. Defines sides a, b, c as arc lengths between vertex pairs. Proves cos(side) = inner product for each side.

sections.title: Part IV: The Dihedral Angle
sections.summary: Defines projectPerp (orthogonal projection onto plane ⊥ to n) and the dihedral angle at vertex C via arccos of normalized inner product of projections.

sections.title: Part V: The Spherical Law of Cosines
sections.summary: The main results. inner_decomposition proves the key algebraic identity. norm_projectPerp_sq and norm_projectPerp_eq_sin establish ‖proj⊥‖ = sin(arc). spherical_law_of_cosines_algebraic and spherical_law_of_cosines_trig give both forms of the theorem.

sections.title: Part VI: Properties and Corollaries
sections.summary: Symmetry of the decomposition, degenerate triangle cases (vertex coincidence), and proj⊥(n,n) = 0.

sections.title: Part VII: Small-Angle Limit
sections.summary: Documents how the spherical law reduces to the planar c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cos(C) via Taylor expansion in the small-angle limit. The planar law of cosines is stated for reference.

conclusion.summary: Fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms) proof of the spherical law of cosines in 341 lines with 24 theorems and 4 definitions. The central technique is inner product decomposition relative to a unit reference direction: ⟨u,v⟩ = ⟨u,n⟩⟨v,n⟩ + ⟨u⊥,v⊥⟩, which directly yields the spherical law when translated to trigonometric notation via cos(arcLength) = ⟨u,v⟩ and ‖proj⊥‖ = sin(arcLength).
conclusion.implications:
The spherical law of cosines is the foundational identity of spherical trigonometry. Combined with its dual (the law of cosines for angles), it allows solving any spherical triangle — the basis of celestial navigation, geodesy, and satellite positioning.

The formalization demonstrates that the inner product decomposition approach cleanly separates the algebraic core from the trigonometric interpretation, making the proof coordinate-free and generalizable to higher-dimensional spheres.
openQuestions: Prove the dual spherical law of cosines for angles: cos(C) = -cos(A)cos(B) + sin(A)sin(B)cos(c)
Formalize the spherical law of sines: sin(a)/sin(A) = sin(b)/sin(B) = sin(c)/sin(C)
Show the spherical excess formula: Area = A + B + C - π, connecting angle sums to curvature
Prove the small-angle limit rigorously using Taylor remainder bounds
Unify Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic laws of cosines as curvature-parametrized family

crossReferences.description: The spherical law of cosines generalizes the planar law of cosines to curved space. In the small-angle limit, cos(c) ≈ 1-c²/2 recovers c² = a²+b²-2ab·cos(C). Both use the same inner product decomposition but on flat vs curved geometry.

The hyperbolic law of cosines cosh(c) = cosh(a)cosh(b) - sinh(a)sinh(b)cos(C) is the negative-curvature analogue. Together, the three versions (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) form a curvature-parametrized family.

The Pythagorean theorem is the planar law of cosines with C = 90°. On the sphere, the 'spherical Pythagorean theorem' is cos(c) = cos(a)cos(b) (when C = π/2), which differs from c² = a² + b² due to curvature.

The area of a spherical cap (the sphere's analogue of a circle) can be computed using the spherical law of cosines. The Gauss-Bonnet theorem connects the spherical excess A+B+C-π to the enclosed area.
